question.prompt:
A round table has radius \(4.\) Six rectangular place mats are placed on the table. Each place mat has width \(1\) and length \(x\) as shown. They are positioned so that each mat has two corners on the edge of the table, these two corners being end points of the same side of length \(x.\) Further, the mats are positioned so that the inner corners each touch an inner corner of an adjacent mat. What is \(x?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2008_AMC_10A_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The touching inner long sides bound a hexagon. First we show that the equal mat dimensions force this hexagon to be regular.

[Figure 1](figures/2008_AMC_10A_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

Let \(O\) be the table's center. Every outer long side is a chord of length \(x\). The perpendicular from \(O\) bisects each chord, so all these chords have the same distance \(d\) from \(O\), with
\[
d^2+\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2=4^2=16.
\]
Each rectangle extends from its outer chord toward the center, since extending away would put its other corners outside the table. Its inner midpoint is one unit closer along the same perpendicular line. Its distance from \(O\) is therefore \(|d-1|\). Consequently, every inner corner has the same distance \(R\) from \(O\), where
\[
R^2=(d-1)^2+\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2.
\]
Thus the inner hexagon has six equal sides and all its vertices on a circle centered at \(O\). Equal chords give equal minor arcs. None of the six consecutive gaps can instead be the corresponding major arc: that gap together with the other five would exceed a full circle. Hence the six central angles are all \(360^\circ/6=60^\circ\), and the hexagon is regular.

Joining \(O\) to its vertices now gives six equilateral triangles, so \(R=x\). Since the inner corners lie on the table, \(x\leq4\). The first equation then gives \(d^2\geq12\), so \(d>1\). This establishes that the inner side is at distance \(d-1\) from \(O\).

Bisecting one of the equilateral triangles produces a right triangle with hypotenuse \(x\) and one leg \(x/2\). Therefore the distance from \(O\) to an inner side is
\[
\sqrt{x^2-\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2}
=\frac{\sqrt3\,x}{2}.
\]
Adding the mat's width gives \(d=1+\sqrt3\,x/2\). Substituting into the radius equation yields
\[
\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2+
\left(1+\frac{\sqrt3\,x}{2}\right)^2=16,
\]
which simplifies to
\[
x^2+\sqrt3\,x=15.
\]
Completing the square gives
\[
\left(x+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2=\frac{63}{4}.
\]
Because \(x>0\), the expression inside the square is positive, so only the positive square root is admissible. Thus
\[
x=\boxed{\frac{3\sqrt7-\sqrt3}{2}}.
\]
This value is positive, is less than \(4\), and satisfies the radius equation. The answer is choice \(\boxed{\mathrm{C}}\).
solutions.title: The inner hexagon and a radius triangle
